utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The case, IT-04-74-PT, the Prosecutor against Jadranko Prlic, Bruno Stojic, Slobodan Praljak, Milivoj Petkovic, Valentin Coric, and Berislav Pusic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. There's no need to say good afternoon again, but I would like to have the appearances again, that is, for reasons of the record. Mr. Scott, you're representing the Office of the Prosecution, with the same team as I saw before during the Status Conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then as far as the accused are concerned, Defence is concerned, Mr. Olujic, you are there as counsel for Mr. Stojic. Mr. Par and Mr. Salahovic are there as counsel for Mr. Prlic. Then Mr. Kovacic and Ms. Pinter are there to defend Mr. Praljak. Ms. Alaburic is there as Defence counsel for Mr. Petkovic. Mr. Jonjic is there as Defence counsel for Mr. Coric, and Mr. Skobic, you're there for the defence of Mr. Pusic. Then we have two -- I must say four persons who are not present. There seems to be a problem with the translation with one of the representatives of -- I do not know yet which government. Yes. For this hearing, a hearing on six motions for provisional release, the governments of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia have been invited. May I ask you to introduce yourself. Perhaps first on my right-hand side. Could you please put on the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HALILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am Mevludin Halilovic, minister of the interior of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I'm the authorised representative of the government of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Halilovic. And you are accompanied by?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRISTO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm Borjana Kristo, the federal minister of justice, and I am going to orally present the guarantees that the government has granted at its sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Halilovic and Ms. Kristo. I then guess that you're representing the government of Croatia. Could you please introduce yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MULJACIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Jaksa Muljacic, assistant minister of justice, representing here for the Status Conference for provisional release in the accuseds' matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Muljacic. And you are accompanied by? Or you are in the company of?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRNIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm Croatian Ambassador Frane Krnic, also authorised to represent the interests of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You now registered your presence in a written message. Thank you, Mr. Muljacic and Mr. Krnic. We will now -- I first would like to inform you that the Bench is not complete. The decision on provisional release will be taken by three Judges. The Judges assigned to the cases of all six of you are Judge Liu, who is president of Trial Chamber I, who is sitting to my right, who's Presiding Judge, although I'll preside over this hearing, and Judge El Mahdi, who is, for urgent reasons, not present, but who has read all the written submissions and who will of course read the transcript of this hearing and make himself acquainted with whatever will be said this afternoon. As far as I'm concerned, my name is Alphonse Orie. I'm the judge. But we have been in the hearing already once before. That was at the Initial Appearance. The absence of Judge El Mahdi is under Rule 15 bis of the Rules of -- this Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence. This Chamber has received a motion by the Prosecution which is a confidential motion, but with the consent of Mr. Scott, I can say in public that this motion aims at deferral of the decision to be taken on the six motions for provisional release. If there would be any further argument needed on that, we do that in private session. We have carefully examined and studied all your submissions and a lot of attachments to it, and I'd like to remind you that there's no need to repeat anything that has been said in these written submissions. The scope, therefore, today of this hearing is to see whether there are any new arguments which the -- you would like to bring to the attention of this Chamber; that is, argument in excess or in addition to what has already been stated in the written submissions. You, Mr. Praljak, Pusic, Prlic, Coric, Stojic, and Petkovic will have an opportunity to address the Chamber briefly if you would like to do that on the issue. If there's anything you would like to add to what counsel then has already said. May I remind you that you are then supposed to strictly limit yourself to the issue at stake at this very moment. Let me first give an opportunity to the Defence of Mr. Prlic to address the Chamber with any additional arguments. Mr. Salahovic or Mr. Par. Who is ...? Yes, Mr. Salahovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAHOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, the Defence has initiated this procedure and applied for the provisional release of Jadranko Prlic until the beginning of trial. Allow me to provide you just with a general overview of our application. We started from the position that the accused Jadranko Prlic is in the pre-trial detention and that this pre-trial detention is of a special nature and that it has lost it for a certain period of time. We are also starting from the position that the accused may be provisionally released until the beginning of trial and that he is entitled to have that right granted to him. At the same time, it is certain that this right of his is in your hands. It is your discretional right and it is founded and stems from the Statute of the Tribunal, from its Article 65 [as interpreted], and the mission that has been given to you. As Defence counsel for the accused, we don't have any doubts whatsoever that it is up to us and to the accused to convince you of two things. Firstly, that the accused is not going to abuse this right; and secondly, that he is worthy of your trust. We fully appreciate, although this is entirely in the hands of every Trial Chamber, that in addition to that, the Defence has to achieve a standard of proof. In all that, in addition to relying on the law, we also rely on the case law of this Tribunal. The case law of this Tribunal has shown that this Tribunal fully takes into account all the internationally adopted standards regarding the rights of the accused. A number of accused have been provisionally released until the beginning of their respective trials, and this is still the case. A number of decisions taken by this Tribunal has put the interests of the accused first, bearing in mind also that their decision should not be prejudicial and detrimental for the future of the trial. That is why we deem that it is very important for us to mention the case of Ademi, in which the Trial Chamber has decided as follows: The Trial Chamber has to interpret Rule 65, taking into account the facts of every particular case, but also the very specific situation that an individual is being put in. In addition to that decision, I would like to say something else. When this Rule is interpreted, one has to take into account the general rule of proportionality. The procedural measures should never be excessive if it suffices to use a lesser measure, then a lesser measure should be used. And finally, detention is not punishment. Its nature is not punishment. And since the accused enjoys the right to be considered innocent, Your Honours, we, as Defence counsel, are not convinced that it is necessary or indispensable to keep Jadranko Prlic in detention until the beginning of trial. In addition to that, we are absolutely convinced that it would be appropriate for him to await trial on provisional release. It would be appropriate because such a decision of yours would only establish that Jadranko Prlic will not abuse this right. It is also appropriate because everybody has to believe in the justice of this Court, because it's the foundation of every trial. In addition to that, Rule 22 -- 20 of the Tribunal puts the rights of the accused first, and the need to protect victims and witnesses is second. It is also appropriate, Your Honours, because such a decision that you might take may -- will not be unjust in anybody's eyes. It will not be unjust at the detriment of the Defence, of the victims, of the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or the international community in general. And finally, Your Honours, I would like to mention and emphasise a principle, the principle that would be the guideline for the Defence during the trial. Despite the burden that all the parties in the trial bear as their responsibility, there is no need to behave in any other way but bona fide. As far as the Prosecutor's reply is concerned, I can say only this: One should not ignore the specific situation that every individual is and that one should rely only on the evidence whose reliability is not questionable. And finally, the dual approach should be ruled out, especially the automatic approach, the administration of justice. And finally, Your Honours, I would like to give the floor to my colleague Mr. Par who is going to mention the specific nature of the indictment. He will take the time that he has left into account and he will try to use it as efficiently as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, Mr. Salahovic, first of all, I invited you not to deal with matters that are already clear on paper. Am I wrong that the attention you've asked us to pay to the Ademi case that I find already in paragraph 7 of your submission for provisional release, isn't it true that we find there already a long quotation from that case, from the Ademi case?

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAHOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have understood, and of course you are not mistaken. However, I have taken the liberty, taking into account that this procedure is the procedure against the accused. This is our first appearance before you, to provide general principles of our application. In this, we have also taken into account your decision. I apologise to you if we have mentioned this decision in our written submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's automatic. I just wanted to remind you that we would very much like to hear additional argument. But since you kept it quite short, there's no real problem. When you refer to Article 65 of the Statute, may I take it that you refer to Article 65 -- to Rule 65 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAHOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I believe I have. I've mentioned Rule 65 of the Rules and Article 20 of the Statute. We can double-check if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was translated to us as "Article 65" of the Statute. But that has been clarified now. Then I have one final question before I give an opportunity to your colleague to address the Chamber. You said in the Statute it's the rights of the accused first and, for example, rights of victims only second. Is that your interpretation of the sequence in the Statute, or are there any other reasons to assume that what comes first is most important?

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAHOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I really did say that, but this is just one part. And this is just what I read in a decision of this Tribunal. And I believe that this would be a short way for me to say what I wish to say. And if you want me to, I can even quote the decision that I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would please give me the decision so that we can check it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAHOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you would just bear with me for a second, I would like to consult my colleague. This is a decision taken by this Tribunal in the Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic case, and the decision was taken on the application filed by Momir Talic on the 28th of March, 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. Salahovic. Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAHOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. My task is to use the following five minutes and convince this Trial Chamber that it would be appropriate to provisionally release Jadranko Prlic until the beginning of trial. Jadranko Prlic meets all the requirements of Rule 65, and the Defence has proven this by the guarantees provided by the state, by personal guarantees, and international guarantees. The two states in question are the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They have provided a guarantee saying that in case Jadranko Prlic is provisionally released, they will use it their repressive mechanisms in order to ensure the presence of Jadranko Prlic before this Trial Chamber if this is necessary. In their response, the Prosecutor has doubted the guarantees of the Republic of Croatia openly, quoting some past times, some past governments, and past political relationships. We are now in the year 2004. The Croatian government has been commended for its cooperation with The Hague. This has been confirmed by the President of this Tribunal, by the Chief Prosecutor of this Tribunal, and the Security Council of the UN. This has also been confirmed by the European Union. The current Croatian government is capable of arresting Jadranko Prlic at any given moment, whenever it is asked to do so. It is also capable of preventing Mr. Prlic from fleeing. It is also capable of preventing Mr. Jadranko Prlic from jeopardising this procedure. This has to do with this government's compliance with its international commitments. I'm very sure that the high representatives of the Croatian government who are present today in this courtroom will confirm my words and provide you evidence in order to corroborate those words. I have the same position with regard to the guarantees provided by the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but I'm sure that one of my colleagues will say more about that. In addition to the state guarantees, we have also attached two types of personal guarantees. One has to do with the family of Jadranko Prlic. In this guarantee, his wife and children inform this Trial Chamber about their circumstances. Jadranko Prlic will reside with them in Zagreb. Together with him, they will share the burden of this trial, and they do not have any secret plan on escaping or starting a new life elsewhere. Jadranko Prlic is a family man. He's a teacher, a professor. He has a Ph.D. in economics. He is a diplomat. His life and work is connected with the university and the parliament benches, and there is nothing that would point to the fact that he will escape, that he will become a renegade, that he will become -- that he will in any way obstruct the work of this Tribunal. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, they're aware of that. In Croatia, they're aware of all that. And the international community is also aware of that. The highest representatives of the international community in Bosnia and Herzegovina, who have worked there between 1995 and 2003, Mr. Carl Bildt, Mr. Wolfgang Petritsch, and Mr. Westendorp, have also given Mr. Prlic their guarantees and they have been provided to this Tribunal. Carl Bildt said in his guarantee that he supports Mr. Prlic's application for provisional release wholeheartedly. And Mr. Petric also confirms that. Carlos Westendorp claims that Jadranko Prlic may be trusted and that he is fully capable of honouring all the decisions of this Tribunal. The high officials of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Ivandic, Lagumdzija have given their guarantees, saying exactly the same. The only person who doesn't trust Jadranko Prlic is the Prosecutor. In their response, they say, and they portray Jadranko Prlic as an individual who is involved in some deals and some persons who are involved in such deals. The Prosecutor says that the accused will escape, that he will go into hiding, and the message of the Prosecutor to the Trial Chamber is not to release Jadranko Prlic. Contrary to that construed picture, which is not based on any evidence, here before us we have the real Jadranko Prlic, a professor, a scientist, a Croatian politician from Bosnia and Herzegovina who is pro-European in his orientation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You announced that you would take five minutes. I think, although my computer is not working well, that we're over the five minutes now. Could you please conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will conclude with saying just a few words, Your Honours. I have said all this because today we're talking about the risk of provisionally releasing this man until the beginning of trial. The Defence believes that it has offered facts that remove this risk. And I'm going to mention just a fundamental fact. Let's not forget that Jadranko Prlic volunteered to appear before this Trial Chamber and that this fact shows the kind of relationship that Jadranko Prlic has with this Tribunal. He wants to stand trial in order to defend himself, and this is what -- this proves the Prosecutor in the belief that Jadranko Prlic will escape. That's why we would like to ask the Trial Chamber once again to provisionally release Jadranko Prlic until trial. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Par. Mr. Olujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is Olujic, actually. Thank you, Your Honour. In our motion for provisional release, we have presented before the Trial Chamber all the reasons, all the arguments that this Trial Chamber will weigh and consider once they retreat, in order to decide to grant or not this motion. However, it is my duty to point out certain additional facts, or rather, emphasise that, among other things, my client is an elderly man, as you can see. After the period of indictment, he completely abandoned political life and public life in general. He was never part of political life or any organisations or army organisations after that period. He does not have any financial means which are a prerequisite for fleeing. He surrendered voluntarily to this Tribunal. He never said a word against this Tribunal. He has no prior convictions. Therefore, Your Honours, I have to invoke the law that prevails in this high institution. I know that you are aware of it, but it is precisely in the argumentation, the Statute, and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence that govern our work in this Tribunal that indicate that my client should be provisionally released. It is an element of Roman or civil law, the legal system where we come from, and in my written submission, I invoked all the relevant legislation by articles, including also a special provision of the Croatian legal system which is house arrest. The government of the Republic of Croatia is prepared to guarantee that he will be under house arrest in Croatia if necessary, and available to you whenever required. What are the provisions of the Rules of Procedure? That an accused has the right to be provisionally released pending trial, with certain limitations under Article 22 of the Statute. Nothing limits the Trial Chamber in this respect; on the contrary, it gives it the possibility to provisionally release the accused, because it says the accused can be provisionally released only under the Trial Chamber's decision. The Republic of Croatia is prepared to do everything that the Tribunal requires if such a motion is granted. Your Honours, I will shorten my presentation and mention only one more thing. To prove before you today that all the arguments presented by the esteemed Office of the Prosecutor can in no way apply to my client. The Prosecutor says, and the case-law of this Tribunal knows, that onus probandi lies on them. But we cannot prove in advance something that is yet to be alleged. That would be contrary to common sense and every law. The Prosecutor further objects to the provisional release by trying to change the scope of allegations and narrowing it down. We have provided all the financial evidence and all the factual evidence proving that Bruno Stojic has residence in Croatia. That is already in evidence. But it is illogical to claim that because Bruno Stojic did not have to hunt for Bruno Stojic -- that Bruno Stojic did not have to be hunted for by the Croatian government, he should not be provisionally released. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. It is not fair to link the issue of the capture of Mr. Gotovina with the provisional release of Bruno Stojic. Let me summarise, Your Honour. For the past ten years, my client has nothing to do with politics, with the army, with the police, or any appearance in public. He knows that proceedings are under way against him, and as soon as he learned of the indictment against him, he surrendered himself voluntarily. Let me stress one more thing. In my view, the best way to achieve all the tasks of this Tribunal with respect to the former Yugoslavia is to provisionally release Bruno Stojic, because if released, he will be a living vehicle of the message that if indicted, one should come to the Tribunal and orally present their defence. Let me quote one more example from the Republic of Croatia, and that is General Ademi. He has already sent the message I refer to to the entire world. It is being felt both in the Croatian public and in this Tribunal. However, the message of the ICTY is, in fact, we are looking for justice and truth, and we are offering respect for all the rights of the accused. My client is the best example for this, with his family situation and his political background. That is why we move that he be released from the detention of The Hague Tribunal and returned to Croatia, with all the guarantees involved. Or, alternatively, that he be placed under house arrest, which would be a 100 per cent guarantee that he will respond to every summons. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Olujic. May I invite next Mr. Kovacic or Ms. Pinter. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will try to avoid the trap of repetition in relation to our written reply to the response of the Prosecutor or in our original motion for provisional release. I will try to confine myself to the quintessence and additional arguments which for one reason or another have not been mentioned yet. One of the arguments invoked by our learned friends from the Prosecution, in paragraph 19 of their response to the motion for provisional release of Coric, and it is a general argument applied to all the accused, namely, that the Republic of Croatia may not, after all, be able to live up to their guarantees because a discussion is pending in the Croatian parliament which could, they say, change the political balance and the attitude of Croatia toward this Court. Why do I begin with this? This discussion has just taken place in the Croatian parliament. The decisions and materials have been taken and made. I see that the Prosecutor is in possession of them. And this discussion took the best part of a day. Its conclusions go in the direction that all the activities under way have to remain geared towards full cooperation with the ICTY. Not only did not this discussion -- this debate in the parliament jeopardise the Croatian cooperation with this Tribunal; it actually confirmed the Croatian parliament's commitment to keep it that way. Let me just remind you that, in the recent past, eight accused have surrendered to the ICTY, and at least a part of the credit for that has to go to the Republic of Croatia and its policy of good faith. As my colleague Mr. Olujic said, the Ademi case is significant and relevant because it had spread the message in Croatia and indicated to the indictees in Croatia that they can expect a fair trial and respect of their rights. My client, Slobodan Praljak, surrendered voluntarily upon his own initiative as soon as he learned of the indictment. He reported to the Ministry of Justice, he collected the indictment himself, and he travelled to The Hague himself. There were no arrangements involved on anybody's part in bringing him here. The Prosecutor, in his response, questions this obvious argument, saying that maybe the accused will change his mind when he learns of the evidence. Your Honours, can we really accept the claim that a serious, well-educated man, with two university degrees - excuse me - three university degrees, a man who has been an intellectual all his life and a professional, can he really surrender just because he thinks that there is no evidence against him? No, we could not accept that. He surrendered because he believed that he would be able to defend himself against that evidence. What sense would it make after this voluntarily surrender for him to return to Zagreb and then change his mind, without even seeing the supporting material and seeing how things are, he may not see it for a long time yet. And this brings me to a new argument which has not been mentioned in our written submission, the balance of the various rights of the accused. On the one hand, he is entitled to an expeditious trial. On the other hand, we all know that he will not get an expeditious trial very soon here, because this case involves six accused, and the Prosecutor is not prepared to go into the courtroom and start the trial, as he should be, even before issuing an indictment, not only under the Rules of this Tribunal but under the legislation of every civilised country with a decent legal system. The Prosecutor, once having issued the indictment, has to be ready to start the trial the next day. We know this is not the case here. Finding the right balance between an expeditious trial and the right of the accused not to be in detention awaiting trial for too long a time is the question here. We can assess the realities and fairly conclude that both the requirements from Rule 65 are satisfied here. It was common knowledge in Croatia for quite a long time that this indictment could well be issued. Mr. Praljak has been aware for a long time that investigation is targeting him and that an indictment is very likely. What did he do? He did not run away. He did not try to hide. He did not try to tamper with the witnesses. The Prosecutor is very well aware of this. There is no indication that his prior associates, friends, or acquaintances ever tried to contact anybody in relation to the allegations in the indictment. If this has not happened in the past six years - maybe I'm exaggerating. Maybe it's only four years since Mr. Praljak learned that there is an investigation against him - why would he start doing this now, after returning home? That, however, is still a theoretical possibility, and that is why we suggest that if the Trial Chamber grants this motion, there are further restrictive measures available. Although I have mentioned Ademi, it is indubitable that one of the duties of this Tribunal is to spread a positive message, not only in their judgements and convictions of individual persons for individual crimes in those wretched wars in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, but also to spread the message of the existence of fair trials, the message that all national legislations, as well as the European convention, endorsed. Among other things, the detention should be chosen only when other measures are insufficient. I shall only remind you of the provisions of the ICC concerning detention, which are on a much higher level, and even the Croatian national provisions from 20 years ago. The case-law of this Tribunal is something that I am not going to invoke again, but it is, and remains, a fact that voluntary surrender has to be taken into account adequately. And let me add one more thing which I don't believe we said clearly enough in our written submission. It is not so much the guarantees of the host country and the country to which the accused seeks to be released that the Court has to decide upon. The Trial Chamber has to decide upon the facts, which are very well known in this case, and it is well known that even if the estimate of this Tribunal proves to be wrong, the Republic of Croatia will do its utmost to ensure all additional security. Thank you for your attention, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kovacic. Ms. Alaburic. May I remind you that where you were all invited to stay within approximately five to ten minutes, that two out of the three of you until now, I'm talking about accused or Defence teams rather than individual counsel, took already more than ten minutes. So may I please ask you to stay within the time limits indicated to you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. If somebody were to ask me to use one word, yes or no, in answer to the question whether the indictment requires for Mr. Milivoj Petkovic to be in prison or to be provisionally released, I would say that he has to be provisionally released. The indictment does not argument [as interpreted] that for a single reason, not for a single moment does the Prosecution claim that my client Mr. Petkovic would run away from Croatia or that he would go into hiding somewhere else and that he would not respond to the Tribunal's summons to appear before it. Not only do they not give any -- offer any evidence, they don't even claim that. The Prosecution doesn't even claim that my client in any way obstructed the investigation against him, that he prevented the Prosecution from collecting evidence, that he tried to influence the prospective witnesses, victims, or any other person. It is from this indisputable fact that serve as the starting point for our conclusion that the Prosecution confirms that all the conditions from Rule 65(B) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence have been met and that my client has met the criteria provided for by this provision. I would like to say just one more thing that have to do with the application of law. During -- it will be Rule 65(B) that will be governing Rule in this, as well as the international jurisprudence on human rights, primarily the right to freedom, the presumption of innocence, and the measures of legal protection. When we're talking about right of an individual to freedom, I would like to point out as very important that according to the practice of the European Court for Human Rights there is a fundamental difference between the fundamental reasons for an individual to be detained in comparison with the fundamental reasons for the detention to be prolonged for the person who is already detained. Namely, during the investigation, or at the beginning of trial, when -- of procedure when a person is being arrested and detained, the following legitimate legal interests have to be protected: Prevent of the illegal influence of this person on either witnesses, victims, or destruction of evidence. The second legitimate reason is to prevent the repetition of a crime or the completion of the crime. The third legitimate purpose is to prevent the disturbance of the general public, and the fourth legitimate purpose is to ensure the presence of the accused during the trial. Once the investigation is completed, once the evidence is gathered, once the witnesses and victims have been heard, once the indictment has been issued, many of those reasons that justify detention stop existing. We are in the stage of the procedure when the indictment was issued, which means that the OTP has carried out the investigation, has listened to potential witnesses, has interviewed victims, and for that reason the justified reasons for detention have stopped existing as regards those elements. That's why at this moment the only legitimate issue that we have to discuss is whether there is a probability or a guarantee that the accused, if provisionally released, will indeed appear before Trial Chamber. I would like to repeat that the Prosecution has never doubted for a second that my client, Mr. Milivoj Petkovic, will appear before this Tribunal. I would like to point to the position of the European Court on Human Rights in the case Wemhof against Germany in its paragraph 46. If the fear and the failure of the accused to appear before the Trial Chamber is the only reason for detention - I apologise for speeding - if the fear for escape and the consequential absence of the accused from trial is the only reason for detention, then the accused has to be provisionally released if he can provide guarantees that would ensure his presence. Your Honours, if you deem that the guarantees that were provided by my client, both his personal guarantee and the guarantees of the state, are insufficient, then we would like to move for his detention to be prolonged, but the place of detention to be changed, and instead of being detained here in The Hague, that he should be released to house arrest. I thank you for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Alaburic. Mr. Jonjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before I summarise our arguments corroborating our motion for the provisional release of Mr. Valentin Coric, allow me to remind everyone present that our Defence has not yet had the opportunity of formally objecting to the motion of the Prosecutor to defer the decision on provisional release --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jonjic, it is -- are you intending to make any written submissions in that respect or would you like to deal with it now? Which is quite welcome. But as you know, it is a confidential motion, and with the special consent of Mr. Scott, I mentioned what the motion was about. But I wouldn't go in public, go into any further detail in that respect. So if you'd like to address the Chamber in that respect, I'd rather ask for private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I did not mean to go into the details of our objection, but to deal with a discussion that took place at this morning's 65 ter meeting. I only wanted to say that the Defence objects, but we can present our arguments either in writing or orally after this is finished, as you decide. Now let me briefly present our arguments in favour of the provisional release of Mr. Coric. For reasons of economy, the Defence of Mr. Coric, mutatis mutandis, subscribes to the arguments presented by our colleagues, all the more so because the legal basis for these was given in the motion for provisional release of the 7th of June and the 12th of July. In these, the accused Valentin Coric has provided valid corroboration of his request to be provisionally released. Even before the indictment was issued and this indictment was the subject of innuendo in Croatia for seven years, my client indicated that he's prepared to contact the Prosecutor's office in Zagreb. He decided to do so without any contacts with any political authority in Croatia. It was only on his own initiative and at his own responsibility. After the indictment was delivered to him, he was able, both in practice and hypothetically, to flee, but he never decided to do so, although it was very clear from the indictment itself that he would be found guilty under that indictment -- that if he is found guilty under that indictment, he would be facing a severe sentence. One of the arguments offered by the Prosecutor against our motion for provisional release is the need to defer disclosure of supporting material. My client has no wealth, as the Prosecution seems to indicate through press coverage, and my client has tried to refute them. My client has a two and a half-year-old daughter, born after 17 years of marriage, which is an additional reason for my client, Valentin Coric, to become even more closely linked and bound to his family, which would make him available to this Tribunal at any moment. After the events cited in the indictment, my client occupied high positions in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, he never jeopardised the safety of witnesses or the course of justice. And after the Office of the Prosecutor, shortly after my client's Initial Appearance, asked for protective measures for witnesses, my client agreed with those measures without any hesitation, as well as with any other measures that would ensure the safety of witnesses and their interests. All the claims of the OTP that go against the personal guarantees of Valentin Coric are refuted by hard evidence. None of these claims proved true. However, should the Trial Chamber not grant the motion for provisional release, our client suggested in his submission of the 7th of June house arrest as an alternative. In this way, he demonstrated his readiness to appear before this Tribunal at first request, as well as the fact that he poses no risk to victims and witnesses. The Defence has also deemed necessary to provide evidence that, although our client has no real estate in Croatia, he has a sister owning an apartment in Zagreb who is prepared to take him in. Our learned friends from the OTP already expressed their arguments, casting doubt on the validity of the guarantees of the Republic of Croatia. However, this Trial Chamber very recently concluded that the Republic of Croatia is able to comply with these guarantees very efficiently, such as in the Norac case. We do not see why the same guarantees that apply to Mr. Norac would not apply to our client. If Mr. Coric is released into Bosnia and Herzegovina and the place of release is left by this Defence team in the hands of the Trial Chamber, then we must say that the guarantees of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina have proven to be very effective in the past two years, as we have seen from the examples of General Halilovic, General Hadzihasanovic, and the accused Kubura. The representatives of the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina are present here, and they will certainly uphold their own guarantees. As to the arguments of the Prosecution that the guarantees of the Federation are not valid on the territory of Republika Srpska, we have to point out that a significant step forward has been recently made in this direction. New regulations have been adopted by the relevant ministries, assuring the security over the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So it would seem that it is not decisive which part of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina is in question. However, I repeat: There is still the possibility that the Trial Chamber decides that our client should remain in detention but under house arrest. If that is so, all these arguments become irrelevant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jonjic. Did I understand you well that you said that even that the guarantee of the Federal Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina would be valid or also effective on the Republika Srpska territory?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The guarantees of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina may be implemented in the territory of Republika Srpska, owing to the changes in the legislation and in the personnel that have taken place over the past year or so. A ministry for security has been established, covering the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Minister Halilovic, the minister in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina is here and I'm sure he will be able to provide you with many more technical details of that than I possibly could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The question was mainly not about whether there were structures there, but whether it would be effective as well. Because the validity issue I fully understand, but the effectiveness of ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am deeply convinced that, theoretically speaking, or hypothetically speaking, that it would be proven that the bodies of the Federation are effective in the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jonjic. Mr. Skobic, you're last, but I would say not least.

utterances.speaker: MR. SKOBIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honours. Thank you very much. Your Honours, I accept the general circumstances that have been pointed out by the previous speakers that also apply to my client. According to Rule 65(B), the accused has to convince the Trial Chamber that he will appear for the trial and that he will not pose threat for victims and witnesses and other persons. This is a burden that lies on the accused, and it's a heavy commitment. The Defence wants to get into the structure of this commitment and analyse it from the aspect of his objective capabilities at his disposal. Mere --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Skobic, when you're reading, it's -- you're speaking a bit quicker and the interpreters might have some difficulties in following that. I know that I'm restricting your time, but at the same time, could you slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SKOBIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll try and be of assistance in that respect. Most transparent occasion for the accused to show this subjective attitude are his guarantees, the wish for freedom of every individual is extremely great. In this specific case, we are facing the situation which freedom has been denied. And it would be possible to conclude from this situation that any person in such a situation will provide any guarantee whatsoever, committing themselves to comply with anything. The situation is not that simple. A question may be raised here. If we guarantee only on the individual guarantees that the accused has provided, what can he do? He can provide a wide range of guarantees that are expected by him from the Trial Chamber. The standards already exist. And one might conclude that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. a personal guarantee is not so difficult to give. However, if that indeed is the case, then a question may be raised as to how can these be tested in an objective way? How can one be sure that guarantees given will be honoured if there is any sort of temptation? How can these guarantees be given an objective dimension? According to the Defence, the real test for the guarantees given can be applied once the accused is released. However, it is the task of the accused to convince the Trial Chamber that he is true when he gives his guarantees before he is released. Now, how does the Defence see this problem? In the short time the accused Pusic has been in the situation when he could be tested, it was the moment when he faced the indictment and when he was still a free man. It was the moment of the biggest temptation for every man, including Mr. Pusic. The media speculations about the existence of the indictment found him in the clinical centre of Ljubljana in the Republic of Slovenia when he was hospitalised, when he learned of the possibility that he might be indicted against the advice of his doctors, he left his hospital bed, even at the detriment of his health. He left the Republic of Croatia, arrived in -- he left the Republic of Slovenia, arrived in Zagreb. He left all of his contacts and takes the indictment on the following day My question to you is: Can such a man be trusted? If he's provisionally released, that he would respond to the summons of the Trial Chamber? The Defence believes that there is no doubt whatsoever that he will. He has already proven what his attitude towards this Tribunal is, in the following way: Without any second thoughts, without resorting to the excuse of his health situation, in an invalid chair, he arrived in the Detention Unit, where he still is to this very day. In this way, he has proven a very strong willingness to respect this Tribunal, to respect justice, and to present his arguments in his defence only before this Tribunal. The OTP, on the other hand, when they give their views of the willingness of the accused to appear before the Trial Chamber points to two very important elements. One is the evidence that the Prosecution has and the seriousness of the incriminations. The Defence claims that the accused will not change his mind. The accused is aware of the fact that the OTP has evidence that they will present during their case, and that have been collected in a long investigation. However, he believes that he will be able to argue his case successfully and he has received a lot of letters from Bosniak Muslims who have been living as refugees all over the place. According to some claims by the Prosecution, these people are their prospective witnesses. However, they have written to him, and that has reinforced him in his belief that he will be able to argue his case successfully. Nothing has changed from the moment when my client faced the indictment, because he had followed the work of the Tribunal even before that through the Internet. He had been informed about all the indictments, all the final sentences, all the developments. So while he was still a free man, he was absolutely aware of his legal situation. I don't see any reason why anything would change in his mind at the moment when he is provisionally released. It seems to me that the OTP has not provided a single valid argument to that effect. My colleague Jonjic has spoken enough about the guarantees provided by the Government of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Let me just emphasise one little segment that has not been explained in my reply to the Prosecutor's response. I would like to say that the Government of the Federation is the body that provided a guarantee. There is also a guarantee of the canton of Mostar in Herzegovina. But they are not the main guarantor. It is the government. A prosaic question is being raised: What if the accused leaves the territory of that particular canton? What is going to happen then? My reply to that is follows: Nothing is going to happen. The police functions perfectly in the Federation. There is also an inter-cantonal cooperation. It is impossible to imagine a situation in which criminals would just cross from one territory to another and be safe in that other territory just for the lack of coordination amongst cantons. At the end of the day, there are federal bodies. There is the police with their representatives in every place. There is a perfect [as interpreted] of the nation between the federal Ministry of Justice and all the cantons. My colleague Tomislav Jonjic has informed you that an agency has been established in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Its name is SIPA. And one of its principal tasks is the arrest of the fugitives. Therefore, I believe that the guarantees provided are very firm and they have been tested before and we know what the result of these guarantees have been. The four accused have been provisionally released and the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina has honoured all of its commitments, and within that context there have been no problems or objections on the part of the Trial Chamber. Your Honour, at the end, I would like to underline one more element, and that is the health condition of my client, Mr. Pusic. He himself, at the very beginning, said something about that, and I'm not going to repeat any of that, because there is ample documentation of his health. However, one has to ask oneself: How can a person who is using crutches, who has difficulty walking, how can such a person decide to flee or run away? What activities are at his disposal if one is aware of the fact that any escape involves physical strength and physical fitness? Finally, I believe that the accused Berislav Pusic has met all the conditions provided for in Rule 65(B). Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skobic. Mr. Scott, would you like to respond to the submissions? And how much time would you think you'd need for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May it please the Court. My calculations, and of course I'll be guided by the Registry's official accounting, but my notes indicate that the Defence collectively have taken approximately 106 -- excuse me. One hour and six minutes. My apologies. One hour and six minutes. Obviously, the Prosecution would not ask to have that full amount of time, but we do have to respond to a number of arguments that the various six have made. So we would appreciate, Your Honour, having -- we would be satisfied if we had half the amount of time that the Defence had all together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course you'll understand that if six counsel have to represent their clients, that is a lot of specific details which might not all need to be responded to. So if you could -- well, let's say in approximately 20 minutes, a little bit over 20 minutes would be 5.00, if you would be able to conclude --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you'd allow me just to put the stand up on ... May it please the Court, counsel. In the limited time that's available to me, Your Honours, Mr. President, let me perhaps start a different perspective in a short amount of time. You've heard all afternoon about these men do not present any risk of flight or any risk to victims and witnesses in this case. I have to remind the Chamber, with all respect, that while, of course, only allegations at this point, the indictment in this case charges that these men presided over a campaign that terrorised and caused many people, victims and witnesses, to live under a reign of terror for some long period of time, victims who still today remember quite well what happened these years ago, victims that remember today quite well what these six individual did to them, victims that today fear and have concerns about their release back into the areas where these victims and witnesses live. In my 20 years, Your Honours, of doing this work, I must say I've attended a number of hearings such as this, I must -- have -- I have to tell the Chamber, in 20 years I've never heard an accused come in on a provisional or pre-trial release motion and tell you that, if released, I'm going to escape. If released, I'm going to interfere with witnesses. Of course not. Of course we wouldn't expect counsel to say that. And yet we do know in our collective experience, in our collective wisdom, that it happens. Despite the best promises, despite the protest of innocence, and of course they're presumed innocence. Of course, as in all criminal cases. But despite all that, we know it happens. We know that accused flee. We know that victims and witnesses are intimidated, harassed, that there is obstruction of justice in cases. These are not hollow or artificial concerns. I think, Your Honours, that those of us who have practiced here for a while in this particular environment, we lose, in all respect, and I'm speaking for myself as well as everyone else in this courtroom, we lose perspective of what it is we are doing here. We become almost too used to it. We are dealing with the most serious charges, concerning the most horrible conduct in the world that one can imagine. In national systems, I submit to Your Honours, in national judicial systems, a man who kills, who takes the life or is responsible for taking the life of one victim or two victims, in most cases, will be detained pending trial. Not all, but in most cases in most systems. A man who sexually assaults a woman or several women, in most cases, in most systems, will be detained pending trial, including in the country that these gentlemen come from. In Croatia, most people convicted are -- excuse me, charged with serious -- the most serious crimes, the most heinous crimes, will be detained pending trial, including war crimes cases. Surely if in the national systems a person is detained for killing one person or sexually assaulting, how terrible it is, one woman, then surely, surely, serious consideration must be given to detention to men who were charged with being responsible for taking the lives of hundreds of people, for sexual assault on a large scale, for massive arson and destruction of property. That's what we're talking about here, and I don't think we can lose sight of that. And I dare say that in most systems, most accused charged with multiple murders, multiple sexual assault, multiple destruction and arson of property, would be detained pending trial. Your Honour, my comment -- some of my comments may be a bit disjointed given the limitations of time, so I apologise in advance that my -- some of my remarks may not flow as much -- as well as I might like them to. But I would like to touch on a few points and I'll have to jump around in order to do that in the time allowed. The Chamber knows that from its own experiences, that another important factor is the conditions in these states of the former Yugoslavia. We're not talking about conditions on the ground in the Netherlands or in France or in Argentina. We're talking about conditions and circumstances that are still very raw, where law enforcement is still very limited, where all too many people avoid arrest. We're talking about a country, we're talking about the arrests, the Republika Srpska, we're talking about -- which has protected and kept Radovan Karadzic from being arrested for years. We're talking about a situation, you know, on the Bosnian Croat, Croat side where we've mentioned to you several instances, Gotovina, the Rajic case, Mr. Ljubicic. Even assuming for the moment that there was the best of intentions on the part of some of the parties, the states involved, assuming for the moment the best of intentions, the bottom line is the same. Gotovina is not in custody today. He does not stand before this Tribunal, for whatever reason. He's not here. And Rajic and Ljubicic only came after protracted periods of time and in some instances with the direct protection of at least some highly placed persons. This is a place where there are still wartime associations, networks of people, victims are scared. Accused or some of the accused are still regarded by some people as war heroes. It's different than the individual offender international system. It's not going to go out into an environment where there is extensive networks of people only all too ready and willing to support them, all too willing to carry out their will. It's a very different situation. And again, I think that we have to be very mindful of that, and sometimes again I think that those of us who have been here for a while perhaps forget that. We have the world's most heinous crimes, we have places on the ground that are under extremely difficult conditions, and present unusual challenges for pre-trial supervision, and it's in that environment and these circumstances that we are asked to consider the question of pre-trial release. Even in this case already there's been protest, there's been demonstrations, there's been signing petitions, there's been people raising all sorts of issues about these accused. That's the environment that we operate in. Presents -- these things present unique challenges to this Tribunal, unlike most national systems. Turns to the guarantees given by Croatia and certain authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina. We do have serious concerns, Your Honours. They're not lightly given. They're not personally directed at any of the gentlemen or lady sitting in this room. They're institutional issues, they're structural issues about the realities on the ground in these places today, and probably tomorrow. We suggest to the Chamber, respectfully, that a guarantee should be considered -- there's two factors for the Chamber to consider, with respect. One is whether the state can be seen as acting as a bona fide neutral guarantor, in the place of a guarantor to bring these people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Skobic, is there ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SKOBIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would kindly ask you, my client is signalling me that he should go to the bathroom. Can this be granted to him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As far as security is able to accompany him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SKOBIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's also having certain difficulties. He is experiencing certain difficulties. He's not feeling too well, I've just been told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you want us to have a break? Because we'll have to have a break anyhow. We could take it now, because we're running out of tapes. Perhaps the best way of doing it is to ask Mr. Scott to finish after we have a break of, I would say, 15 minutes. Yes. We'll then have a break for 15 minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. SKOBIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are not insisting on a break, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but we have to -- we have to have a break anyhow, because the tape is only running for one hour and 45 minutes. So at 5.00, when we have not heard yet the representatives of the Government of Croatia and of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we would have to have a break anyhow and I would have one or two questions. So we'll have a break until 5 minutes past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give an opportunity to Mr. Scott to continue: Mr. Pusic, are you well enough to attend? You don't have to stand if you ... Do you feel better?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, yes, and I can attend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please inform me, either by yourself or through counsel, if you feel that you're not able to attend or that any measure has to be taken.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honour, before the break I was touching on two separate considerations, both equally important in considering the guarantees of all of the authorities that are involved here, and I started to say, one is whether these states or authorities can be considered to be acting as a reliable, neutral guarantor. And a second and separate consideration is whether they can be considered a reliable and effective law enforcement agency. Because that in effect is what we're asking them to do. Since the Tribunal does not have a police force of its own, we have to rely on essentially the police force, the criminal justice system of these states or authorities to do for us, for the Tribunal, what we are not able to do for ourselves. That creates a very important question, a very important question. Quite apart from the goodwill or best intentions of the states or authorities involved here. I just want to mention in passing that I think even the term "guarantee" that we use is a bit of a misnomer. With all respect, none of the parties, none of the states that are here today can guarantee that any of these accused will come and appear in the future if released. They can make their best efforts, they can state their best intentions. None of them can guarantee that they won't flee or that they won't interfere with witnesses. In terms of the first question, whether they can be viewed as a neutral guarantor, as a fair guarantor, it is true, and perhaps unfortunate, that the Prosecution does have serious concerns and questions about the status of the state of Croatia as a neutral guarantor for these accused, and I'll have to move quite quickly, Your Honours. First of all, it is true that the Tribunal has had a very long and very difficult history with Croatia, as with some of the other states in the former Yugoslavia. Now, of course, there are people who would just as soon forget that history, but I'm sorry, it's not that easy. A few months of improved dealings does not simply wipe away years and years of obstruction, delay, and making life difficult for this Tribunal. Since March 2004, many of Croatia's most senior government and political leaders, including the prime minister, the president of the parliament, have made high-profile public statements opposing the Cermak/Markac indictments and opposing the indictments in this case, calling the indictments or at least parts of the indictments unacceptable to Croatia. They've talked about creating -- trying to intervene as a party in the case, becoming an amicus curiae in the case, supporting these defences actively, financially, with legal resources, forming teams of experts to assist the Defence, collecting documents to assist the Defence, doing everything possible to get these men provisionally released, timing political decisions so as not to prejudice the posture of these men before the Tribunal, delaying debates in parliament so as not to put their positions at a disadvantage. In some respects, Your Honours, in some respects, Croatia begins to appear more and more like a co-party with the accused than a neutral guarantor. Now, lest our position be misunderstood, some might say, well, Croatia has every right to do those things. Perhaps. Perhaps it does. Perhaps it can side -- it can do whatever it wants -- with the accused, can fully support them as much as it wants to. But it's still a fair consideration for this Chamber to say: If that's the case, can we -- they really be considered as a neutral guarantor or are they really a party taking on the character of a party? On the ability side, Your Honours, again, a separate consideration. The Chamber need not decide -- the Chamber is not inclined to do so. The Chamber need not decide or express a view on the good intentions of the Croatian government. But even assuming for the moment good intentions, there's a second element, and that is the effectiveness, their ability to make good on their commitments. And that's completely separate from the question of good intentions. And then, sadly, there again we had the examples, and there could be others, but we had the examples of Ivica Rajic avoids arrest for eight years during which part of the time he was being paid and on the salary -- on the payroll of the Croatian Ministry of. We have the case of Pasko Ljubicic, who avoided come into custody for 14 months. We have the Gotovina situation, still a fugitive. Maybe it's Croatia's best intentions to get Gotovina here, but he isn't here, and that trial can't start until he is here. The Defence teams have stated that much of this evidence is not relevant that because many of these actions relate to what might be called the Tudjman government. But Your Honours, Mr. President, Judge Orie, of the three examples that I've just given to you, all of those began or continued under post-Tudjman governments. I'm sorry. You can't run away from your history just quite so quickly. In terms of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and again, moving extremely quickly, we just make a few basic points. No guarantee has been given by the state or national government. As the Chamber knows, we have the two entities, the Federation and the Republika Srpska. There is a national government, there's a three-member Presidency and there are some national agencies or ministries, a few. Under the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it's the national entity, it's those limited state -- at the state level that is responsible for meeting the international obligations, including the production of war criminals under Dayton to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. international community. We don't have a guarantee from the national or state government. The proposed national police, SIPA, state information and protection agency, which some counsel referred to, is on the drawing boards and steps are being taken to put it into effect, but it is not a functioning agency at this time. And if time allowed, I would give -- I would take the Chamber to recent assessments by the office of the High Representative, by United States ambassador, by a report to the European Union police mission, saying those things. It's not an effective national police force yet. We hope it will be some day, but it's not now. There's no guarantee that's been given by the Republika Srpska, and while one might wonder whether one of these men, a Bosnian Croat, would move over into the Serb side, it's happened, and we all know that, unfortunately, unfortunately, Republika Srpska becomes a black hole for people trying to avoid this Tribunal. Still trying to get Radovan Karadzic, years later. There's no guarantee from the Republika Srpska. Finally, and I'm only going to be able to touch on it. In terms of the canton, the Ministry of Interior of the Herzegovina Neretva canton, we have a guarantee from one canton. Obviously it's only as good as the boundaries of that canton. If any of these gentlemen go into another canton, it has no effect. And there are serious -- we've noted a number of discrepancies, Your Honours, we've gone through again the guarantee given by the canton, contrasted it with information given by several of the accused, and there are a number of discrepancies and I just simply don't have time to go into them all. But that raises again serious questions about the reliability of the Federation or the canton to act as the law enforcement agency for this institution. Can we really believe, even with good intentions, that they can ensure that these men will be here some time from now? Can we really be sure that they will prevent victims and witnesses from being harassed? In closing, Your Honours, if I can just look at my notes. I apologise for going so fast. It is always a challenge, Your Honours, for a party to, an advocate to anticipate that the court might rule against the party, because of course our position is, as we've stated, our position is that each of these men, for the reasons stated, should be detained pending trial, and indeed in most national systems would be detained. But if the Chamber is not so inclined, and again, we hope the Chamber will consider and adopt our position, and the Chamber is of course completely in the Chamber's hands [as interpreted]. If the Chamber is not inclined to do that, then we would request the Chamber to impose the strictest possible conditions on the release of these men. We strongly oppose their release into areas where there are victims and witnesses in this case. We would strongly oppose any wide freedom of movement. I have not had a chance to talk directly with the representatives of the state of Croatia, but if I can communicate indirectly with them, Your Honour, when the Court inquires, I'd be curious their position are they prepared is the state prepared to carry out and enforce house arrest for all six of these accused? At least four of the accused, as I read their pleadings, at least four of the accused have said that's an option. And I would be interested in the state of Croatia's views on whether they're prepared to carry that out. The Chamber might also wish to consider bail. Frankly speaking, there's very little information about these men's financial positions. Which again just -- shows again the difficulty of collecting information in this environment. There is some -- there are significant indications that at least some of these men have very substantial wealth. The Chamber in those circumstances may wish to consider whether to impose some sort of financial bail in addition to any other conditions the Chamber would set. Your Honour, we appreciate the Chamber's indulgence and the time that's been allowed to the Prosecution to state its views ever so briefly. It's our position that these men should be detained, for the reasons stated. If they are not detained, then we beseech the Court, in the interest of the victims, in the interest of witnesses to come, that the strictest possible conditions be imposed, and that in fact if the Court is not inclined to keep them in Scheveningen, that indeed it should be considered whether house arrest in Zagreb is an option. Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honour Judge Orie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I've got one question for you. You're talking about the indications that some of the accused might have a considerable wealth. Are you referring to the articles where I remember that one of the attachments was that journalists are describing who is owning what and who has an interest in what, and is that what you're referring to? I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's primarily -- unfortunately, Your Honour, and -- yes. To be perfectly transparent, that's our main -- that's the main point. Certainly we've heard things from other people and in the field. Witnesses tell you things. And I'm not -- I'm not going to stand here and tell the Chamber that our information is more precise or more certain than that. But I would just say again that that indeed illustrates part of the very problem we're addressing here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. But since you are talking about bail, do you want the Chamber to impose bail on the basis of newspaper or --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, probably not. Probably not. But I do think, and I would invite the Chamber with all respect to make what additional inquiries the Chamber may be able to make. The Chamber may have access to information or means that we haven't had, at least up till now, and I would invite the Chamber to at least consider that. I think -- well, you know, there's the old saying, where there's smoke there's fire, and I think there are sufficient indications that some of these men do have substantial wealth, but I agree, up till now, the Prosecution has not been able to show that in any definitive way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Scott. Before I give an opportunity to the representatives of the governments, I would like to ask a few questions, first of all to you, Ms. Alaburic, in respect of Mr. Petkovic. We have seen in the response by the Prosecution that reference is made to a transcript of a meeting which has taken place quite some time ago, where a certain Mr. Miljevac reports about a meeting he would have had with Mr. Petkovic, and the subject of that meeting was the testimony of Mr. Petkovic in the Blaskic case. I've also seen that Mr. Petkovic denies that -- ever to have expressed himself in the way as reported. Could you assist the Chamber in explaining why Mr. Miljevac would have come up with such a story which seems at first sight to fit well into what the meeting is about? Why would he have invented such a story? Is there any explanation, as far as you are concerned, apart from saying Mr. Petkovic never expressed himself in that way?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I personally do not know Mr. Miljevac at this meeting held on the 13th of April, 1999, according to the transcript. I did not attend it. And it is difficult for me to say for what reasons Mr. Miljevac expressed himself as he did about his indisputable conversation with Mr. Petkovic. I don't know why he misinterpreted it and misrepresented it. I can only, based on the contents of that transcript and the context of the report of the intelligence community of Croatia from 1998, as well as on the basis of what I know as a regular citizen of the Republic of Croatia from our media, press, and other sources, I can only surmise what it is about. The team of people who was, in a way, in charge of monitoring the cooperation of the Republic of Croatia with the ICTY, because, as you know, Croatia had an office for this cooperation and the highest officials of Croatia were represented in that office. As far as I was able to discern from those transcripts, the office tried to assist the defence of various accused by providing them with documentation, and from the transcript that I read, the intelligence community seems to have tried to ensure that within the framework of individual defences, the interests of Croatia are protected. Based on that documentation, I believe that Mr. Miljevac who was then-minister of defence, wished, concerning the testimony of Mr. Petkovic in the Blaskic case, was speaking about the way this intelligence community regarded this testimony in the Blaskic case. I can only invoke one part of that transcript, where my client is spoken about in the following way: "He is not one of us. He doesn't belong to us. He's not from our circle." So I cannot find out, even through General Petkovic, what the motives could be for Mr. Miljevac to say what he said in the presence of Mr. Tudjman, except to surmise that when the highest officials spoke with Mr. Tudjman, tried to present themselves in the best possible light, tried to portray themselves as working very hard for the interests of Croatia. What I believe matters most in this case is whether my client, Mr. Petkovic, really said that or not, or, as the Prosecutor claims, he perjured himself in the Blaskic case. We can take the transcript of that testimony and, based on the contents, we can decide whether he really testified to the best of his knowledge and recollection, or he lied against General Blaskic and against Croatia. And I emphasised in my written submission that if the Trial Chamber deems this issue worthy of discussion, I suggest that the testimony of my client in the Blaskic case should be obtained, so that we can discuss it in closed session. And then the Prosecutor would be able to show us what specifically is untrue in my client's testimony. And I wish to say that I am particularly sorry that if the Prosecutor already wanted to say that my client perjured himself, he didn't say so openly. Instead, they used another person's statement to cast doubt on my client's truthfulness. I don't believe this is appropriate. If the Office of the Prosecutor intends to discredit my client, or anybody else, they should come out openly. I wish to point out once again that the Prosecutor did not have any objection to my client's testimony in the Blaskic case, and it is only now, at this hearing on provisional release, that this doubt in the truthfulness of my client is being questioned. If any further explanation is required, I am at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it was a bit of argument, in addition to the answer to the question I put to you. But thank you for your answer. Since you initiated some argument, I might give an opportunity to Mr. Scott, too, then, but then very briefly, respond. Then I also have a question for Mr. Salahovic. We have seen -- and I'm asking Mr. Scott first of all a clarification. Is it true that the transcript of the minutes of a meeting of the 16th of September 1998, which you provided as attachment D in relation to the motion by Mr. Petkovic, was it also provided directly in Mr. Prlic -- in the answer to Mr. Prlic's motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise, Judge Orie. We're having to track that down a bit. We're getting it. The -- there were the minutes of a meeting on the -- in 1999, and I believe that was attached to the response concerning Mr. Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. That's true. But there was also attached minutes of a meeting in September 1998. I think you're referring now to the annex B to it. But let me just check.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think it is, to the Prlic document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Attachment D in the Petkovic response. Was that also filed in Prlic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think it was. I think that that attachment was also in the Prlic response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have a question to you, Mr. Salahovic. The Prosecution has presented a transcript of the minutes of a meeting where Mr. Prlic was present, and, well, let me say -- let me try to say this softly, if possible, that the atmosphere of that meeting, at first sight, was one of a high level of interest on how Defence counsel would behave in the defence of the cases of the individuals. And in this transcript, we do not see any observation by Mr. Prlic that he would oppose against such an atmosphere, where it is suggested that a defence should not be just for the person, for the accused, but should be coordinated, well coordinated and should be -- all the lawyers should be under one umbrella, is just one of the lines that, according to this transcript, was spoken. Another line is: "I talked to some people, but I think that those lawyers cannot work on their own and defend as they do from one case to another." This is what I take as lines creating an atmosphere where the individual responsibility of counsel is not a prevailing value, but rather, that there is some control or at least some influence sought over how counsel behave. I do not see any response or any opposition by Mr. Prlic. Could you address that matter, which you did not address in your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAHOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have tried to understand, and I wish to say this: When I presented our case to you earlier today, I wished to emphasise that I always place faith in the evidence which have been checked for authenticity and credibility. I believe that the transcript in question does not have these qualities. And that is why I accepted with some reservations. Further on, I wish to say as follows: I really don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I then immediately put a question. You say the authenticity of this transcript seems to be doubtful to you. Did you seek any confirmation by the Prosecution where it comes from and how it came to the Prosecution? Because that could support your idea of not being authentic. I mean, what did you do to verify the authenticity or the non-authenticity of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAHOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have approached this in good faith. This paper, in my view, does not contain the basic elements of what it should contain.
