I really have not expected that it will be accorded so much significance. I would only like to say something about what you have asked me, just one sentence, if I may. I don't see from this conversation that Mr. Prlic advocated any sort of control, persuasion, pressure, that would be against the rights of the accused before this Tribunal to freely present their case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Salahovic, my question is quite simple. I did not ask you -- I did not even suggest that Mr. Prlic said anything on that subject. I have drawn your attention to the fact that there was a discussion where Mr. Prlic supposedly had been present, and that during this conversation, some participants in that conversation took the position that you just couldn't -- that counsel go and do what they deem fit, but that -- well, they should be under one umbrella, which is to be understood as a way of interference with how individual counsel think they should conduct the defence. I asked you to address the matter of the silence of Mr. Prlic, who was present, and who did not say: No, that's not something you could do. Or: That's not fair. That's up to Defence counsel to defend each individual as he deems fit. That's the issue I'm raising, not that Mr. Prlic himself did express any illegal matters. But perhaps the first question: Do you think that intervention in individual defences, is that, in view of you, is that legitimate or is it not legitimate?

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAHOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will be very brief. I am against any interference with the work of Defence counsel. I've understood your question. This paper shows that Mr. Jadranko Prlic did not support those positions. It transpires from that paper that he didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where do I read that? If you say the paper does not show that he supported it, but the paper also does not show that he opposed against it, although being present at that meeting, let's just assume that he -- that the transcript is authentic enough to establish that - it's neither of the two, isn't it? You say the paper shows that he did not support. Where do I read that he did not support?

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAHOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that the mere presence -- I don't believe that the mere presence at the meeting is support. He has not expressed his views on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said, Mr. Salahovic: "This paper shows that Mr. Jadranko Prlic did not support those positions." What you are saying now is that his mere presence does not mean that he supports the words spoken by others. I fully agree with that. But you said something different. You said the paper shows that he did not support. Or was it that you wanted to say the paper does not show that he explicitly supported or that he supported at all the words spoken by the others?

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAHOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. You have asked me quite a number of questions. Kindly bear in mind the fact that -- what the circumstances of that meeting were. The persons involved in the meeting were those who had power, who had force, and due to such circumstances, I would like to draw the following conclusion: Silence equals opposition to any of the positions that may have been put forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's your interpretation of the silence. Thank you. Would you like to add something or is this what you'd like to say in respect of this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAHOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have nothing else to raise at this particular moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I would first like to give an opportunity to the representatives of the government of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Ms. Kristo, did I understand that you will confirm orally the guarantees, or at least the commitment of your government that has already been given in writing? If so, I'd like to hear that. And if you could also perhaps address the issue of what I now understand to be the SIPA, the state information and protection agency, on which some counsel have reported.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRISTO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will orally present the guarantees that the Government of the Federation has already given for the accused Jadranko Prlic, Bruno Stojic, Valentin Coric, Berislav Pusic, and Slobodan Praljak. I take this opportunity to express the willingness of the Federation to guarantee that the Government of the Federation is going to comply with all the summons of the Trial Chamber and that it will honour all the conditions that are given to the accused by the ICTY. Should the Trial Chamber of this Tribunal decide to act on Rule 5 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and take decision on provisional release of the accused and decide for these persons to be -- to reside in the territory of the Federation, I guarantee on behalf of the Federation that the Federation will make sure that the accused will respond to every summons of the Tribunal, in The Hague or in any other place determined by the Trial Chamber. Also, we guarantee that we will carry out any of the orders of the Trial Chamber. I would also like to take this opportunity, Your Honours, that we would like to provide additional guarantees, and I would like to express the willingness on the part of the Government of the Federation in terms of the compliance with any additional conditions that the Trial Chamber of this Tribunal may impose on the Federation that will lead to the provisional release of the accused pending trial. I claim this as a responsible person and as a member of the Government of the Federation at the head of the Federal Ministry of Justice, and I'm saying that the institutions of the Government of the Federation have carried out all the actions and have complied with all the commitments taken over by the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina within its cooperation with the Tribunal. The Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina has all the institutions and instruments by which it can provide for all of the orders of this Trial Chamber to be carried out in time and for all the other conditions to be complied with. Thank you very much. Should there be any additional questions, I'm at your disposal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I missed something, but one of the issues that had been discussed by counsel was how effective the Federation could act if someone would not be on federal territory any more, but in Republika Srpska. And in this relation -- in this context, the state information and protection agency has been mentioned, I would say in a more encouraging way by Defence counsel, and a bit less encouraging way by the Prosecution. Could you inform the Chamber about effective -- how effective the Federation could be if someone would abscond to the Republika Srpska territory. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRISTO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I fully understand your question and I must say that I would like to express my optimism on this issue. The government are functioning at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which means that the entities are duty-bound to cooperate with the state ministry of security. They have cooperation with Interpol. So all the orders can be executed effectively and efficiently, in keeping with any of the conditions that may be imposed. I believe, and I hope, that you have been able to convince yourself of such compliance with regard to the former provisional release guarantees that the Government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina has given in the previous cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for your answer. You mentioned the five accused, not Mr. Petkovic. That is correct? You did not give any guarantee in relation to Mr. Petkovic? It's only the Croatian government that has provided guarantees in respect of Mr. Petkovic. Yes. Could I then invite you, Mr. Muljacic, to address the Chamber and to confirm, if possible, the written guarantees already given, and as I understood from the minister of justice of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina that it was, I would say, an unlimited guarantee to the sense that whatever condition the Chamber would impose, it would be followed by the government. Could I hear the position of the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MULJACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I may take an opportunity to speak in my own language, with your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MULJACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. In my capacity as assistant of the Ministry of Justice and Mr. Frane Krnic, the ambassador of the Republic of Croatia in the Netherlands, would like to orally confirm the written guarantees signed by the minister of justice of the Republic of Croatia given to the Croatian citizens. Mr. Bruno Stojic, Mr. Milivoj Petkovic, Jadranko Prlic, Slobodan Praljak, Valentin Coric, and Berislav Pusic that the government of the Republic of Croatia will comply with all the orders of the Tribunal with regard to their appearances before the Trial Chamber in case of their provisional release. The government of the Republic of Croatia will also undertake all the measures in order to ensure that the aforementioned gentlemen stand trial and that in case of provisional release they will not present a danger for any potential witness, victims, or any other individuals. The Republic of the Government of Croatia is prepared to provide any additional guarantees that might be needed for their provisional release. Mr. President, Your Honours, if you will allow me, I would like to refer to several things that have been said by the Prosecution with regard to the cooperation of the Republic of Croatia with this high court. This cooperation has already been assessed by the Chief Prosecutor, Ms. Carla Del Ponte, His Excellency, Mr. Meron, the President of this Tribunal, as being full and complete, and this was done before the highest bodies of the international community. The Republic of Croatia really fully cooperates with the Tribunal and it is willing and as a state with a rule of law, it guarantees that should this Trial Chamber make such decision, it is willing to comply with any orders of the Trial Chamber in respect of this decision. I would also like to say a few words on other things mentioned by the Prosecution. With the new government, headed by Prime Minister Senada [phoen], new priorities have been set out and one of the priorities is full cooperation with the Hague Tribunal. The prime minister himself announced it and one of the first moves on the part of the government was to move that cooperation from the political field to the ministries, respective ministries, the Ministry of Justice and the Ministry of the Interior. And from then on, the cooperation has indeed been full and complete. The government of Croatia indeed cooperates with regard to the accused, to the witnesses, to the documentation, in keeping with the Statute and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. On several occasions, the Chief Prosecutor, Mrs. Carla Del Ponte, has stated that whatever was promised in January has been delivered. Croatia cooperates fully and is given as a role model for all the other states in the region. This doesn't mean that Croatia does not have the right to protect its own interest. The fact is that when the indictments were issued against Generals Cermak and Markac and the accused present here, the prime minister sent a letter to the Tribunal without mentioning anybody's individual responsibility. Because this is up to the Chamber to decide that. In these cases, the Republic of Croatia has been emphasised as the state whose international responsibility is put in question. This letter was sent to the President of the Tribunal, asking for his legal opinion. The President of this Tribunal says that the Republic of Croatia is entitled to protecting the interests of its citizens, that there is an institute of amicus curiae in this Tribunal, and when the trials start, the Republic of Croatia can apply for the status of amicus curiae, and as such, address certain political qualifications. It would indeed -- the indictment which are not acceptable for Croatia [as interpreted]. Therefore, throughout this time, the Republic of Croatia and its government have been fully cooperating with the Tribunal in The Hague, having full respect for all its institutions, the rules and regulations of this Court, and the Tribunal as such. I therefore believe, Mr. President, Your Honours, that the guarantees given by Croatia will be complied with. Republic of Croatia has already given guarantees in the Ademi and Norac cases. In this case, again, we believe that Croatia would be able to comply with all the orders that the Trial Chamber may take in this case as well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have one specific question for you. As some counsel and also the Prosecution have raised the possibility of house arrest, that is, a restriction of movement, even more that we very often see, so not just stay in your village or report every day to the police, but stay in your house. Could you inform the Chamber about the practical possibilities for such a house arrest, and could you inform the Chamber about whether there are any legal obstacles to impose such a house arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MULJACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Croatian legislation is familiar with this institution and will fully honour such an order should it be taken by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even at the request of a foreign institution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MULJACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I put the same question in respect of the house arrest to you as well, and the Minister Kristo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRISTO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to ask the same question, whether it would be practical, possible, and whether it would be -- whether there would be any legal obstacles in imposing house arrest.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRISTO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Government of the Federation is prepared to execute all the decisions, including any additional orders the Trial Chamber may take to secure provisional release for the said accused. That means that there are no legal obstacles for the execution of any order or meeting of any standard set by this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I was informed that Mr. Prlic would like to address the Chamber personally. If there are any other wishes -- within certain time limits, I will allow the individual accused to address the Chamber, to the extent they wish to do so. Mr. Prlic. Yes, you're on your feet, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Kovacic, Your Honour. Mr. Praljak just gave me a sign that he would also like to use this opportunity, just only two or three sentences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I first would like to invite Mr. Prlic to address the Chamber and then Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Starting to use my two minutes, I wish to give my word of honour before you personally that in case I'm provisionally released, I will appear whenever requested to do so by this Tribunal, that I will comply with every order, and that I will in no way interfere with the course of justice. In case of provisional release, I will reside in Zagreb in the apartment where my wife and children are. I would continue with my research work in political economy. I would be supported financially by my wife and by the proceeds from my research and scientific work. In the past 15 years towards my native state of Bosnia-Herzegovina and my fellow citizens, I have displayed a conduct that shows that I can be trusted. I have made my decision independently, and my voluntary surrender is a logical consequence of my entire conduct. I found myself in a situation which decides on my future, but also that of my family. My family and I will defend our honour before this Tribunal, and that is a choice I've made that has no alternative. What I have to do here is to prove that I am not guilty, that the charges against me are unfounded, and that I am not responsible for the crimes I am charged with. I can do that only before this Tribunal. Therefore, there is no fear and no risk that in case of provisional release I should change my mind and obstruct these proceedings. The arguments corroborating and supporting my motion have been presented in writing and orally. The only thing I wish to add is the following: There is not a single person whatsoever who is more anxious to appear before this Court than myself. If the charges levelled against me are not disproved, my further life has no sense at all. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Prlic. I'd first like to give an opportunity to Mr. Praljak. I promised that he would be given an opportunity. Mr. Praljak, please. And if you stay as nicely within the two minutes as Mr. Prlic did, then it would be highly appreciated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be even briefer than that, Your Honour. Facts, first of all. My name, as a possible indictee, has been bandied about in the territory of the Republic of Croatia even before the Blaskic case started. Therefore, I knew for years that I was a possible indictee. It was not, of course, easy to live under this constant pressure that the media put on me. You might be leaving as soon as tomorrow. I have gone through many interviews, and in each of them I was asked the question: If asked to appear before the Tribunal, would you? I always said yes. I had many interviews in Zagreb, in Banja Luka, in Mostar, and my answer was always yes. I always knew that the Tribunal prefers high officials from each of the concerned states. I knew that the charges are complex, and if I had had any intention to flee, I would have done it much earlier. Instead, I patiently waited here. However, unlike Mr. Prlic, I will not be proving here my innocence. I remain innocent, on the contrary, until I am proven otherwise. I was a Croatian general. I occupied many posts and positions. I am proud of everything I've done in my life, and nothing will prevent me from defending before this Tribunal my entire life and my entire work. In that sense, the Court can rest assured that I will appear here whenever requested. It is only logical that a person who is a few months shy of 60 believes that the Detention Unit, where you have limited communication with your family, is much worse than provisional release. I have no intention to flee from provisional release. Therefore, I came here to defend myself and whatever I did in my native state. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. I really beg your pardon, but my client, Mr. Petkovic, has just signaled me that he would also like to address you, very briefly, and I ask your leave for him to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic. You've got two minutes as well. When I say that you nicely stayed within the two minutes, I mean to say that you usually take two and a half, up to two three quarters. Could I also invite you to stay within the time limits. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. Like General Praljak, I too can say that I have lived for seven years now under the burden of possibly being indicted by this Tribunal. On two occasions, I have responded to the summons of this Tribunal. I know what kind of charges have to be answered here and I know what sentence one faces if found guilty. In all those seven years, I have not once thought of fleeing. Instead, I decided to come here. The very process of my extradition went this way: The minister of defence informed us of the indictments, and somebody asked us whether we would go within seven days. We said - it was Friday then - we would go as soon as Monday. Get us the tickets. In my appearances, in my public appearances, I have never expressed a single negative opinion against this Tribunal. I am a law-abiding and loyal citizen of the Republic of Croatia. I uphold its efforts to cooperate with this Tribunal. And as a regular citizen and an official of my state, I support it in everything. I will not obstruct in any way the efforts of my state to join the integration processes in Europe. Therefore, I will remain at your disposal and will respond to your summons at any time. One more thing. I would not dream of leaving Croatia, because my wife was -- had just undergone surgery for cancer and she needs postoperative treatment. So I will remain either here in Scheveningen or in Republic of Croatia and you may rest assured that I will promptly respond to every summons I receive.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, my client Mr. Bruno Stojic would also like to address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, equality before the Court for everyone. But I give that opportunity to you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED STOJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- not after I had expressed my wish that your wife recovers well, Mr. Petkovic. Please proceed, Mr. Stojic. Since Mr. Petkovic is not wearing his headphones, he might not have received my wishes, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED STOJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will take even less time, Your Honour. I did not mean to be long. I agree with everything my Defence counsel said. I never had any intention of fleeing, nor will I ever run. I didn't think when I was going to The Hague that it was that kind of prison. All sorts of rumours circulated. It's not as bad as rumour had it. It looks more like a home for the elderly than like a prison. I am physically able to withstand it and I really assure you that I will return here whenever requested to do so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jonjic, yes. It's the inevitable, I would say. I take it that Mr. Coric also would like to address. Yes. Mr. Coric, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. My predecessors have already expressed most of what I wanted to say. I just want to add: I came here to defend my honour and nobody can take away my right to do that. So I will duly comply with every request to appear before this Court if my motion for provisional release is granted. In my life, I lived in two states. I was especially attached to Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. In addition, I travelled in the past years throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina and I never had any problem. I was involved in the case of the matter of Jozo Leutar, a former minister, and the trial of the Mostar group. I responded to the summons of this Court and I never interfered with any witnesses. I hope that you will grant my motion and thereby ease the situation of my family in the future. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Skobic, you are not going to tell me that Mr. Pusic would like to address the Court as well, isn't it? Mr. Pusic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I apply for provisional release. I would like to go to Mostar, to my family house in Blabuski Herzodovo [phoen] street number 4, in the house which is owned by my in-laws. If that is not possible, can you please provisionally release me to Zagreb to the Drag Ivanisovico [phoen] street. I am also prepared to be under house arrest in Zagreb. My health condition is not good. I still feel pain. I still have problems with my spine. I'm concerned about my health because, due to my stay in the detention, I couldn't go for rehabilitation. Because of uncertainty of the outcome of my treatment, I have psychological difficulties. I will live on the proceeds of my former work. I used to be the general manager of a company. My family will help me. I have three brothers and three sisters who are willing to give me their help and I accept everything that my brother -- my lawyer has said previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pusic. Then, Mr. Ambassador Krnic, I do understand that you'd like to address the Chamber as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRNIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you very much. Your Honours, I would like to draw attention to two details that the Prosecution has presented here today, because it seems to me that they misrepresent the role of the Republic of Croatia that I resent. If I were attending an international conference, I would probably have to file an official protest for such allegations. However, since we are in a courtroom, I would like to express my embitterment, having heard such allegations. At one moment, the Prosecutor insinuated that there was a suspicious partnership when it comes to the Republic of Croatia giving its guarantees. What he said was that the guarantees are given without any second thoughts, that the Republic of Croatia is paying for some services rendered to it by the accused, and the impression has been created in one way or another that the guarantees are not serious. I would like to state the following: The Republic of Croatia is not in any partnership, let alone suspicious partnership, with the individuals who are present here. It merely protects them based on the Vienna Conventions, which gives certain commitments and obligations to Croatia and orders it to protect its citizens. That's the first detail. The second detail is as follows: Actually, the way the Prosecutor denied the seriousness of the guarantees given by the Republic of Croatia boil down to the lack of efficiency of these guarantees. In my view, the Republic of Croatia has provided guarantees only in those cases when it was certain that it could fully stand behind those guarantees. There have been many more citizens of the Republic of Croatia who were charged before the Tribunal than those for whom guarantees were given. General Gotovina has been mentioned and other fugitives who were either at large or arrested or were brought in here after a long time of hiding. I would like to underline that these people have not been provided guarantees by the Republic of Croatia. In other words, the Republic of Croatia will only give guarantees when it can fully stand behind those guarantees and comply fully with the commitments given by way of those guarantees. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krnic. If this would have been a case of the Prosecutor versus Croatia, I would have asked a lot of questions of the Prosecutor. But he already said somewhere in his remarks that Mr. Gotovina is not here, for whatever reason. So I understood this to be that there's no firm blame by the Prosecution on the Croatian government that Mr. Gotovina is not here. So I -- since what the Prosecutor -- counsel for the Prosecution said expressed some doubts, I gave you an opportunity to respond. But let's be -- let one thing be sure: The first thing that counts here is that the accused appear for trial and will not interfere with witnesses, and that guarantees by the government, guarantees are never without risks. I would rather say commitment of governments could only support that. That is well understood and that's the reason why I did not put any additional questions to the counsel of the Prosecution where certainly, as you have demonstrated, some questions could be put to the position he has presented here. This concludes the hearing on the motion on provisional release. We'll have a short break and then we'll continue hearing on other motions. The break, presumably, will take some taken minutes, because the tapes have to be changed again. And then we'll have a short motion -- hearing, which at least in its start will not be a public hearing. We'll adjourn for ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: adjourned at 6.20 p.m., to be followed by an Ex Parte Hearing.
